opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and honestly it's something I think about almost as much as the technical problems.

The first thing I'd say is that a project like Cosmos is not a typical research project. In a classic research lab, you have small groups, maybe two or three people, each chasing their own idea and writing a paper. That model works well for exploring, but building a world foundation model is closer to building a large system. You have data curation, tokenizers, the pretraining recipe, post-training for different physical AI domains like robotics and autonomous driving, evaluation, infrastructure, and then the work of releasing it so developers can actually use it. No single small group can own all of that.

So the way I approach it is to organize around the pipeline, around the major components of the system, with clear owners for each piece. Each sub-team has a well-defined interface with the others. For example, the data team knows what the model team needs, and the tokenizer team knows what latent representation the diffusion or autoregressive models expect. If the interfaces are clear, people can move fast in parallel without stepping on each other.

The second principle is that the team has to be aligned on one shared goal. In research it's very easy for everyone to optimize for their own paper. For Cosmos, the goal is a model that is genuinely useful for physical AI developers. So we try to make the success metric something everyone shares. When the model gets better, everybody wins. That changes how people collaborate.

Third, I try to keep it as flat as possible and very technical at the leadership level. The people making decisions should be close to the experiments and actually look at the results, look at the generated videos, look at the failure cases. In a field moving this fast, if decisions go through too many layers, you're already behind.

And finally, I think you still need to protect some room for exploration. If everything is execution, you stop innovating. So we keep some people looking at the next generation of ideas, new architectures, new ways to use simulation or synthetic data, so that when the current approach saturates, we already have something ready.

It's always a balance between the discipline of an engineering organization and the curiosity of a research lab. I don't think we've found the perfect answer; we keep adjusting it as the project grows.

r002.rationale: It says team members may optimize for their own papers and emphasizes a shared goal, but does not connect decentralized decision-making to diverging efforts.

r003.rationale: The response does not identify information transparency as a way for team members to make decisions in the organization’s interests.

fable-5.1.text:
Organizational design for something like Cosmos—I think the first thing I'd say is that I didn't design it top-down on a whiteboard. It grew out of the problem.

World foundation models require a lot of very different expertise sitting close together. You need people who understand data at scale—video curation, filtering, captioning pipelines. You need people who understand model architecture, diffusion and autoregressive. You need people who understand tokenizers, which is a whole discipline by itself. You need infrastructure and inference people, because if you can't train and serve the thing efficiently, nothing else matters. And then you need people who actually understand the downstream—robotics, autonomous driving—because otherwise you build a beautiful video generator that nobody in physical AI can use.

So the first principle for me is: organize around the pipeline, not around titles. I try to keep small teams that each own a piece end to end, with a clear interface to the next piece. Data team owns data. Tokenizer team owns the tokenizer. If the boundaries are clean, people can move fast without waiting on each other.

The second principle is that leaders need to be hands-on. In a team this size it's tempting to add layers of managers who just coordinate. I resist that. I want the people leading each area to still be reading papers, still be looking at samples, still be debugging. Research changes too fast. If your leaders are one step removed from the actual work, by the time information reaches them it's already stale.

The third thing—and maybe this is the hardest—is keeping everyone pointed at the same objective. With many people, it is very easy for each group to optimize its own metric. The data team gets a better dataset, the model team gets a better FID, but the robotics partner says the model still doesn't help them. So I spend a lot of my time just making sure the end goal is visible to everybody: can a developer in physical AI pick this up and get value? I'd rather have people argue about that than about who owns what.

And finally, I try to protect a small amount of chaos. Some of the best things in Cosmos came from someone who was not assigned to that problem. If the organization is too rigid, you lose that. So I give people room to wander a bit, and then when something works, we reorganize around it. That's how a lot of the structure actually came to be—it was reverse-engineered from the things that worked.

r001.rationale: The response discusses keeping leaders hands-on and avoiding excess management layers, but does not say that concentrating decision authority in a few people creates a bottleneck that slows progress.

r002.rationale: It explains that groups can optimize their own metrics while missing the shared physical-AI objective, causing efforts to diverge.

r003.rationale: It says the end goal should be visible to everyone, but does not explain that transparent information enables team members to make decisions in the organization’s interests.

r004.rationale: It describes giving people room to explore, but does not connect tolerating mistaken decisions with greater willingness to exercise decision-making authority.

astra-6.text:
I think the starting point is clarity: what are we trying to build, and how do the different pieces come together? For a team this large, you can’t have everybody involved in every decision. You need smaller teams with clear ownership, but you also need a shared understanding of the overall goal.

For something like Cosmos, research and engineering are closely connected. A research decision can affect the data pipeline, the training infrastructure, and how we evaluate the model. So I would organize around those dependencies, making sure the people who need to work together can communicate directly.

The balance is giving people enough autonomy to move quickly while keeping the work coherent. And I don’t think organizational design is ever finished. As the project evolves, you have to revisit where the boundaries are helping and where they’re creating friction.

sol-6.1.text:
I think about organizational design starting with the work: what are we trying to accomplish, and how do we divide that into pieces that teams can really own? For a large effort like Cosmos, you need clear ownership, but you also need people working toward a shared technical direction.

Research adds another challenge because you don’t know in advance which ideas will work. So you want to give small teams enough freedom to explore, while keeping them connected so that a discovery in one area can help another team. If every decision has to come through one person, that becomes a bottleneck.

The balance is autonomy and alignment. People should understand what they own, how their work connects to the larger goal, and who they need to collaborate with. And as the work changes, you have to be willing to adjust the organization.
